newsitem.title: UK: Mark gains in Europe before German jobless report.
newsitem.headline: Mark gains in Europe before German jobless report.

text.p: The mark bounced off Wednesday's lows on its European crosses, with traders now looking to Friday's German jobless report for direction.

Mark crosses benefited as the dollar struggled to extend its recent gains against the German currency. Traders were also reluctant to build up more short mark positions amid newspaper leaks of Friday's German unemployment report and before the U.S. payroll report.

"The mark is looking mildly bid, mainly as the dollar is looking a bit top heavy," said Martin De Blocq, sales manager at Nomura Bank. "Also, the market is focusing on tomorrow's U.S. and German jobs figures."

Mark/French franc was quoted at 3.3740/45 at 1020 GMT from 3.3721/26 late Wednesday in Europe. Mark/lira was at 983.30/60 from 981.57/87 yesterday while mark/peseta was at 84.49/52 from 84.42/44 Wednesday.
A report Thursday showed German gross domestic product rose 0.5 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and was up 1.4 percent from a year.

While the year-on-year increase was less than expected, the mark was bolstered after Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the rate would have been 2.75 percent if there had not been three fewer work days in the quarter.

Separately, German industrial orders rose a bigger-than-expected 3.3 percent in April, and were 6.2 percent higher year on year. While the data is known to be erratic from month to month, the rise was far higher than the 0.8 percent expected.

Traders are now eyeing Friday's jobless figures to see whether Germany's economic recovery is still on track. Two German newspapers reported the unadjusted jobless total fell by about 90,000 in May, citing Federal Labour Office statistics.
"We might see a dip in the mark if the German report is weak and the U.S. payrolls number is strong," said De Blocq at Nomura.
Economists polled by Reuters were expecting a 5,000 decline in the seasonally adjusted German jobless total and a 221,000 increase in U.S. non-farm jobs in May.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Thursday's GDP figures were positive and may help the German government's efforts to cut its budget deficit.

Traders have become increasingly skeptical about whether Germany can reduce its 1997 deficit to the 3 percent of GDP required of EMU entrants after Bonn backed down from its plan to revalue the Bundesbank's reserves and get a payout this year.

Waigel said Germany will do its utmost to meet the EMU convergence criteria and that privatisation may be intensified. He also said it would be wrong to talk of a delay to launching the European single currency, the euro.
While traders expect the euro to be launched on time in 1999, they aren't convinced Germany will meet the Maastricht treaty's fiscal goals on a strict interpretation.
This has fanned expectations of a broad EMU, and is seen hampering any mark rebound in the coming weeks, traders said.

"Mark/Europe has come back a bit today as people are beginning to hedge some of their convergence trades in case everything doesn't go according to plan," said a trader at a Japanese bank in London. "But underlying everything, people still want to be long of dollars and short of marks."

Bucking the trend of a stronger mark was the Swedish crown. The crown more than reversed early losses against the mark after the Riksbank said its currency was undervalued at the moment. Mark/crown was at 4.4855/85 from its early high of 4.4925 and 4.4770/00 Wednesday.
